# **linuxcolors: color palettes from the identity colors of the most popular Linux distros** <a href='https://github.com/ikashnitsky/linuxcolors'><img src='inst/logo/logo-linuxcolors-small.png' align="right" width="20%" min-width="200px"/></a>

![](inst/logo/logo-card.png)

`linuxcolors` turns the brand colours of Linux distributions (Ubuntu orange, Arch blue, Fedora blue, Debian red, Linux Mint green, ...) into palettes for data visualisation. They follow the best practices for scientific colour use set out by [Crameri, Shephard & Heron (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-19160-7) and the [Scientific colour maps](https://www.fabiocrameri.ch/colourmaps):

- **Perceptually ordered.** Lightness (CIE L\*) rises linearly and monotonically in sequential palettes. In diverging palettes it is exactly mirrored around a light centre.
- **Perceptually uniform.** Hue and chroma change smoothly, and equal data steps look like equal colour steps. There are no kinks, which would read as false boundaries.
- **Colour-vision-deficiency (CVD) friendly.** Qualitative colours stay distinct under deuteranopia, protanopia and tritanopia. Continuous maps keep their order.
- **Readable in greyscale.** This follows from the linear lightness.
- **No rainbow, no interpolated categories.** Qualitative palettes are never blended. Continuous palettes are interpolated in the OKLab colour space.

These properties are checked by the package's test suite.

## Installation

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("ikashnitsky/linuxcolors")
```

## Palettes

```{r}
library(linuxcolors)
linux_palettes_info()
```

```{r palettes, fig.height=5.5}
show_linux_palettes()
```

**Qualitative** (for categories):

- `main` is the default. It has 8 colours (Pop!\_OS, MX Linux, CachyOS, Debian, Arch Linux, EndeavourOS, Void Linux, Ubuntu), selected among the brand colours in `linux_distro_colors` to maximise the *worst-case* CIEDE2000 distance across normal vision and the three dichromacies. The minimum ΔE is 13.3; the 8 Okabe–Ito colours (without black) reach 6.4. The order is optimised too, so the first *k* colours are as distinct as possible for any *k*. Need more than 8 categories? Colour alone won't keep them apart; facet, label directly, or lump rare groups.
- `neon` has 5 bright colours (L\* ≥ 50) for dark backgrounds.

**Sequential** (dark → light): `ubuntu` (aubergine → orange → cream), `arch` (navy → Arch blue → ice), `mint` (pine → Mint green → pale lime), and the multi-hue `distrohop` (navy → teal → green → amber, in the spirit of *batlow* and *viridis*).

**Diverging** (light centre): `fedora_redhat` (Fedora blue ↔ Red Hat red), `pop` (Pop!\_OS teal ↔ amber), and `ubuntu_mint` (Ubuntu aubergine ↔ Linux Mint green).

In the continuous palettes, brand colours are *anchors*: they set the hue and chroma, and the lightness is recomputed to obey the rules above. The generating script is [`data-raw/palettes.R`](data-raw/palettes.R). The raw brand colours are available in `linux_distro_colors`.

### How they look with colour-vision deficiency and in greyscale

```{r cvd, fig.height=5.5, fig.width=12}
library(colorspace)

sims <- list(
  normal = identity, deuteranopia = deutan, protanopia = protan,
  tritanopia = tritan, greyscale = desaturate
)
pals <- names(linuxcolors_palettes)

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, length(sims)), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5), oma = c(0, 9, 0, 0))
for (s in names(sims)) {
  plot.new()
  plot.window(c(0, 1), c(length(pals), 0))
  title(s, font.main = 1)
  for (i in seq_along(pals)) {
    cols <- linux_colors(pals[i], if (pals[i] %in% c("main", "neon")) NULL else 64)
    cols <- sims[[s]](cols)
    x <- seq(0, 1, length.out = length(cols) + 1)
    rect(head(x, -1), i - 0.9, x[-1], i - 0.1, col = cols, border = NA)
    if (s == "normal") mtext(pals[i], side = 2, at = i - 0.5, las = 1, line = 0.3, outer = FALSE, xpd = NA)
  }
}
par(op)
```

## Usage

`linux_colors()` extracts colours. Qualitative palettes return their first `n` colours; sequential and diverging palettes are sampled evenly:

```{r}
linux_colors("main", 3)
linux_colors("ubuntu", 5)
```

`scale_colour_linux()` / `scale_color_linux()` and `scale_fill_linux()` plug into ggplot2. The scale type follows the palette type: qualitative palettes give discrete scales, and sequential and diverging palettes give continuous ones.

```{r usage-discrete, fig.height=4}
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))

# Qualitative: groups
ggplot(penguins, aes(flipper_len, body_mass, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8, na.rm = TRUE) +
  scale_colour_linux()
```

```{r usage-sequential, fig.height=4}
# Sequential: a continuous quantity
ggplot(faithfuld, aes(waiting, eruptions, fill = density)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_linux("distrohop") +
  coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE)
```

```{r usage-diverging, fig.height=4}
# Diverging: deviations from a meaningful reference, centred with `midpoint`
ggplot(swiss, aes(Agriculture, Fertility, colour = Fertility - median(Fertility))) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_colour_linux("fedora_redhat", midpoint = 0, name = "Fertility\nvs median") +
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "grey90", colour = NA))
```

```{r usage-ordered, fig.height=4}
# Sequential palette for an ordered factor
ggplot(diamonds, aes(cut, fill = clarity)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_fill_linux("ubuntu", discrete = TRUE)
```

## A note on AI helpers

This package was created with the assistance of AI tools, including Claude Sonnet 4.6 via Perplexity, Gemini Pro 3.1 via Gemini and Antigravity. `inst/init` contains the jumpstarter prompts used to conceptualize the package. The main part of the coding was done using Antigravity. `inst/antigravity` contain the implementation plan and walkthrough,`inst/antigravity/session.json` contains the session history. The package logo was created using nanobanana 2 model in Gemini. The redesign of the palettes following scientific colour best practices (v0.1.0) was done with Claude Opus 5.5 via Claude Code.
